false_negatives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential webhook updates an arbitrary row and leaves it invalid

The handler findFirsts on userId plus appId with no orderBy, then updates or creates outside a transaction. userId and appId are not unique: Google's callback always inserts a new credential, and calendar code later loads a specific credential id. findFirst can update a different row than the one in use, return 200, and leave the active token stale. Concurrent deliveries can both miss and insert duplicates. The update only writes key, so a row already marked invalid stays invalid and is skipped by calendar loading even after a successful sync. Decrypted keys are JSON.parsed and stored with no per-app schema check, so a payload that is not the shape that app expects is persisted and breaks the integration on next use.

Lark deletes the credential before credential sync can refresh it

The new sync call sits after the guard that deletes the credential when refresh_token is missing or refresh_expires_date is expired. Credential sync is the path that is supposed to obtain a new access token from the parent when Cal.com does not hold a usable refresh token (parseRefreshTokenResponse even fabricates refresh_token because sync responses may omit it). A webhook-created Lark credential without a still-valid refresh token is deleted on first use instead of being refreshed, and the user must reconnect. If a refresh token is present, the sync Response is still passed to handleLarkError, which requires Lark's envelope, so a normal token JSON body fails the refresh anyway.

No tests for credential ingestion or the shared refresh path

The new webhook can overwrite any user's OAuth credentials, and parseRefreshTokenResponse / refreshOAuthTokens now run on Google, Office 365, Zoom, and Salesforce refresh. The PR checklist says tests were not added, and there are none for a missing or wrong webhook secret, decrypt failure, two credentials for one app, or a refresh that reloads the saved key. A round-trip that refreshes a Google credential and reads it back would have caught the safeParse wrapper being stored; an Office 365 refresh whose body omits refresh_token would have caught the literal "refresh_token" overwrite.

Salesforce token update calls prisma but never imports it

getClient now calls prisma.credential.update after refreshing the Salesforce token, but this file does not import prisma. The name is undefined, so the first Salesforce calendar operation throws ReferenceError once the token endpoint returns OK and never builds a jsforce Connection. Salesforce event create/update/delete is broken for every user as soon as this ships, including installs that never enable credential sync.

Token sync request is unauthenticated

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, a bearer token, or a body signature, and the URL scheme is not required to be HTTPS. The inbound webhook is authenticated, but this outbound call is what returns live OAuth access tokens. The parent app cannot tell Cal.com from any other caller, and user ids are sequential, so anyone who can reach that URL can request access tokens for arbitrary users. A self-hoster cannot fix that without editing this shared helper.

Zoom sync asks for app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom

refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom app id and installed slug are "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts, appId: "zoom"). Other integrations pass the app-store slug (google-calendar, msteams, office365-calendar). The webhook stores credentials under appMetadata.slug, so a parent that keys off the real slug will not find a Zoom credential when Cal.com posts appSlug=zoomvideo, and token refresh for Zoom sync will 404 or return the wrong app's tokens.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is bypassed by case and spaces

The env list is lowercased but not trimmed, and the filter uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) on the raw input. Zod email() does not lowercase, so Banned@example.com is inserted and then mailed when the list contains banned@example.com. A space after a comma ("a@x.com, b@x.com") makes every entry after the first fail to match. Blacklisted addresses that do match are dropped silently; if any other address remains, the handler still returns success, so the client toasts that every submitted guest was added.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check is AND and never matches a real role

isTeamAdminOrOwner requires isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner to both be true. Membership has a single role, so a team admin is not an owner and an owner is not an admin; the branch is dead for normal memberships. Team admins and owners therefore cannot add guests unless they are also booking.userId or an attendee. Collective co-hosts who are only on the event hosts/references (not booking.userId and not attendees) are rejected as well. The bookings UI treats admin and owner as alternatives (isUserTeamAdminOrOwner) and still shows the action, so those users get FORBIDDEN. The check needs to be OR, and other hosts on the booking need to be allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Notification uses the raw guest list, so existing attendees get a new booking email

sendAddGuestsEmails is called with guests, the original input, not uniqueGuests. In email-manager.ts, any attendee whose email is in that list gets AttendeeScheduledEmail (a fresh confirmation plus an ICS REQUEST) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. The dialog never receives the current attendee list, so submitting one already-invited address plus one new address is a normal case: the existing person is not inserted again, but they are still in guests, so they receive a second "you're scheduled" mail and a new calendar REQUEST, which can duplicate the event or reset RSVP. Only the filtered list should be treated as new guests.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest dedup is case-sensitive, racy, and not applied inside the request

uniqueGuests only drops an address when guest === attendee.email against the pre-read attendee list. A@x.com versus a@x.com, the same address twice in one payload, and the organizer's own email are all inserted. Nothing in this path enforces uniqueness, and the check-then-act is not transactional, so two concurrent calls with the same new address both pass the filter and both create rows. Emails are stored with the original casing, so later exact-match checks keep missing them. When every address is filtered, the error is emails_must_be_unique_valid, which is wrong for "already on the booking".

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest emails ignore disableStandardEmails

sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team member, and every attendee. sendLocationChangeEmails just above, and the other senders in this file, return early when eventTypeDisableHostEmail or eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail is set (metadata.disableStandardEmails). The new function does not take event type metadata, and the handler loads the full eventType but does not pass it. Event types that turned standard emails off (workflows only, or privacy) still send booking details and ICS invites when a guest is added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Add guests is shown for past bookings

The new additional_guests action is pushed into editBookingActions, which is nested in bookedActions. bookedActions is not only rendered for upcoming confirmed bookings; it is also rendered for past confirmed bookings (line 554) and past pending bookings (line 553). Those rows can open AddGuestsDialog and call addGuests. Combined with the handler not rejecting ended bookings, that sends confirmation mail and calendar updates for a meeting that already happened. The action should be limited to upcoming accepted bookings.

Attendees are committed before calendar and email, with no recovery

prisma.booking.update createMany commits the new Attendee rows before updateCalendarAttendees and sendAddGuestsEmails. Only the email call is in try/catch, and that catch logs a fixed string, drops the error object, and then the handler still returns success. If the calendar update throws (wrong credentials, provider error), the mutation 500s after the rows exist, emails never run, and AddGuestsDialog does not invalidate the bookings query on error. A retry treats those addresses as already invited and throws emails_must_be_unique_valid, so the guests stay on the booking with no mail and no calendar update, and the user cannot retry. There is no compensation or idempotent resend.

Attendees can fan out meeting invites with no state or guest limits

The only gate is organizer, attendee email match, or the broken team-admin check. booking.status and endTime are never read, so guests can be added to CANCELLED, REJECTED, PENDING, and already-ended bookings. The new mailers always attach an ICS with status CONFIRMED (attendee-add-guests-email.ts line 15, organizer-add-guests-email.ts line 19) and the payload includes the video URL from booking references, so a pending or cancelled meeting's join link is emailed as a confirmed invite. eventType.disableGuests is never read, so this bypasses the public booking form's no-guests setting. ZAddGuestsInputSchema.guests (addGuests.schema.ts line 5) is an unbounded email array, and each new address gets AttendeeScheduledEmail. Newly added guests are stored as attendees, so anyone with a Cal.com account for that address can invite more people. This is an authedProcedure, not limited to the bookings page.

Calendar update uses the actor's credentials, not the host's

The query loads booking.user with credentials and destinationCalendar, but updateCalendarAttendees is called with an EventManager built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). Calendar references store the host credential id. This handler explicitly allows attendees, and the booker is an attendee while booking.userId is the host, so the booker path — a primary use of "add guests" — does not have those credential ids. The host calendar event is then not updated (or the call throws). The same happens for a team admin acting on someone else's booking, and even the owner path only has one user's credentials, so other collective hosts' calendar references are skipped. Guests can be stored while the existing invites still list the old attendees.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR adds an authenticated mutation that writes attendees, updates calendars, and sends mail, and it adds no tests. There is no coverage for the admin/owner/organizer/attendee/stranger matrix, blacklist and case-insensitive dedup, booking status and disableGuests, seated events, or the branch that chooses AttendeeScheduledEmail versus AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. The admin/owner condition is already wrong; a handler test with an admin who is not the host would have failed the merge.

Seated bookings get bare Attendee rows with no seat check

For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, occupancy is tracked with BookingSeat rows tied to attendees. This update only createManys Attendee records. It never creates BookingSeat rows and never compares the result to seatsPerTimeSlot (that value is only copied onto the calendar payload at line 145). Seat counts and the attendee list diverge: availability that counts seats will ignore these people, while the bookings UI and the add-guest emails include them. seatsShowAttendees is not enforced before the full attendee list is emailed. Paid seated events can also gain people who never took or paid for a seat.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount is a lost update under overlapping crons

Both failure paths set retryCount to the in-memory reminder.retryCount + 1 instead of an atomic increment, and the same pattern is in the catch. This route has no lock and does a Twilio request per reminder, so a second invocation can overlap a slow run. Both read the same count, both call scheduleSMS, and both write the same next value, so the stop-after-two-failures cap is not enforced and the attendee can get duplicate texts. A failure write can also raise retryCount above 1 on a row the other run already marked scheduled, which the new deleteMany then removes along with its SID. Use an atomic increment and a conditional update that only matches scheduled false (and the id).

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup is not limited to unscheduled SMS

The new deleteMany branch matches every WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 and does not filter on method, scheduled, or cancelled. This table also holds EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders, and a scheduled SMS stores the Twilio SID in referenceId so a booking cancellation can stop the message. Failure updates write retryCount from the value read at the start of the run and do not require scheduled = false, so an overlapping run of this cron (no lock, one Twilio call per reminder) can set retryCount to 2 on a row another run already marked scheduled and saved a SID. The next invocation then deletes that row only because retryCount > 1, the SID is gone, and a later cancellation cannot cancel the text. The same predicate will also delete any non-SMS row that exceeds one retry. Restrict this branch to method SMS and scheduled false. The comment above the query still says it only deletes past-due SMS, which is no longer what it does.

false_positives.candidate:
Any two errors permanently drop in-window SMS reminders

Every thrown error in the scheduling try, and every falsy scheduleSMS result, increments the same retryCount, and the next cron deletes the row once retryCount > 1. That includes transient failures (Twilio 5xx or rate limits, getBookerBaseUrl, profile lookup), not only permanent ones such as an invalid number. This job loads every unscheduled SMS reminder whose scheduledDate is within 7 days, so two failed ticks during a short outage delete that whole window. Deletion is irreversible and there is no backoff or Twilio error-code check, so those attendees never get the text even after the provider recovers. Count only permanent send failures toward this cap; leave transient errors retryable until the scheduled date.

Catch-path retry update can abort the cron and orphan a sent SMS

The new catch updates retryCount and does not handle that update failing. The try also wraps the update that stores the Twilio SID after scheduleSMS returns a message. If that SID update throws, the catch still treats it as a scheduling failure: it increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false and referenceId empty even though Twilio already accepted the message. Later runs schedule more messages for the same reminder, and once retryCount > 1 the row is deleted, so none of those messages can be cancelled. Separately, if the catch update itself throws (Prisma P2025 when a concurrent run already deleted the row), the error escapes the catch, the for-loop stops, and every later reminder in the batch is skipped. Previously this catch only logged. Guard the retry update, and do not count a failure that happens after Twilio has already returned a message as 'not scheduled'.

Missing phone or empty body never hits the retry limit

retryCount is incremented only inside the branch that actually calls scheduleSMS. If sendTo is missing (SMS_ATTENDEE with a null booking.smsReminderNumber, or SMS_NUMBER with an empty step sendTo) or the rendered body is empty, the handler skips the send and leaves retryCount at 0 and scheduled false, as long as nothing earlier threw. Those rows stay in the unscheduled-within-7-days query and are fully reprocessed, including profile and booker-URL lookups, on every cron run until scheduledDate is past — the unbounded retry this change is meant to stop. Missing numbers are a common permanent failure and never reach Twilio, so they never reach the new delete. Increment retryCount or delete the row when there is nothing to send.

No tests for retry accounting or the delete predicate

This change deletes workflow reminders and adds no tests. Coverage needs to lock the intended contract: scheduleSMS returning null increments retryCount; a thrown error increments it; the row is removed only after retryCount exceeds 1 and only for unscheduled SMS; a successful schedule with a stored referenceId is not deleted; a missing phone or empty body does not remain in the cron until the event time. Without that, the unscoped deleteMany and the silent no-send path will not be caught before they drop reminders in production.

OR retryCount delete cannot use the existing reminder index

deleteMany now ORs an unindexed retryCount > 1 predicate with the scheduledDate predicate. WorkflowReminder's index is (method, scheduled, scheduledDate) and was not extended for retryCount in the schema change. An OR against a column with no index typically forces a sequential scan of the whole table on every cron tick, taking row locks for deleted tuples, including email and WhatsApp reminders this job does not own. Split the two cleanups into separate deletes and add an index that matches the retry predicate so this cron does not scan the full reminder table.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Team/org SQL is never executed; toEqual does not match nested Prisma.sql

The team-scope assertion here, the org-scope assertion around line 332, and the combined-filter assertion around line 429 compare getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions to a single flat Prisma.sql template via toEqual. Those service methods build the predicate with Array.reduce, so the returned Prisma.Sql values array holds nested Sql fragments; flattening happens only when a query is executed, not in the constructor. vitest deep-equality compares that structure, not rendered SQL, so these three tests fail even when the SQL text matches. NOTHING, user-scope, and single-filter cases are flat templates and can pass, which hides the failure mode. The only query actually sent to the database is the user-scope getBaseConditions case (line 481), which is a pure AND and does not use OR or ANY(array). A passing run therefore does not check team/org authorization, array binding for ANY(${ids}), or the operator-precedence bug when these fragments are AND-ed with a date or status predicate. Execute the team and org fragments with $queryRaw (including an extra AND predicate) and assert both included and excluded rows.

Ungrouped OR fragments break AND composition and can skip authorization

Team and org authorization SQL is an OR of two branches with no surrounding parenthesis group: ("teamId" = … AND "isTeamBooking" = true) OR ("userId" = ANY(…) AND "isTeamBooking" = false), built at the reduce in buildOrgAuthorizationCondition (line 173) and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition (line 204). The event-type filter is the same shape: ("eventTypeId" = $id) OR ("eventParentId" = $id) at line 106, also returned without an outer group when it is the only filter. getBaseConditions wraps each side only when both auth and filters are present (line 73). With no service filters it returns the bare authorization fragment here. That is the common insights path: this service only filters eventTypeId and memberUserId, and findMany (which AND-merged arbitrary caller where-clauses inside Prisma, so grouping was safe) was removed. Callers must add the time window themselves. WHERE ${getBaseConditions()} AND "startTime" >= $from AND "status" = 'accepted' is parsed as (team branch) OR (personal branch AND startTime >= $from AND status = 'accepted') because AND binds tighter than OR. Every team booking for that team is included regardless of date or status, so team/org insights over-count and ignore caller predicates. A second composition, WHERE ${getAuthorizationConditions()} AND ${getFilterConditions()}, is the obvious translation of the old findMany AND and is also wrong: it parses as (auth AND eventTypeId = $id) OR eventParentId = $id, so any booking whose eventParentId matches is returned even when it fails the org/team/user authorization predicate. That leaks rows for child/managed event types outside the caller's scope. Wrap every returned fragment, including the final OR and this no-filter return, in parentheses (Prisma.sql`(${fragment})`) before it is embedded. The new tests expect the unparenthesized text, so they lock the unsafe shape in.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty updateMany throws after cache is written

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache finishes by calling SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}). Prisma Client rejects updateMany when data is empty (Argument `data` is missing / at least one field required), and this check happens even on models with @updatedAt, so the call throws every time. The free/busy rows are already upserted before this line, with no transaction, so Google webhook and watch refresh callers see a failure and retry. Each retry hits the Google freebusy API again, rewrites the cache, and throws again, which can burn calendar API quota and mark sync as failed. Passing {} also does not achieve the comment's goal: the settings UI reads CalendarCache.updatedAt (already maintained by the upsert's @updatedAt), not SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. Remove this call, or if a touch is actually required set updatedAt: new Date() explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper writes the wrong env file and is macOS-only

ENV_FILE is the CWD-relative path ../.env, and the script never cds to its own directory. Running bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root (the usual invocation) updates a .env outside the repo, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never set for the app. The update also uses sed -i '' (line 68), which is BSD/macOS sed; GNU sed on Linux treats '' as a backup suffix and does not apply the substitution. cleanup() always exits 0, so a failed URL extract looks successful to a caller.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Expected auth failure is thrown as a generic Error

When the credential is missing or not owned by ctx.user, deleteCacheHandler throws new Error("Credential not found or access denied"). tRPC maps a plain Error to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, so a normal not-found/forbidden case becomes a 500, gets reported as an exception, and is not a TRPCError the client can distinguish. Use TRPCError with NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is always formatted en-US

The last-updated label is built with Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }) even though useLocale() is already in this component and the string is translated. Non-English users see an English date format (and the key is not formatted with their locale), which is wrong for a new user-facing timestamp in an i18n app.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status treats expired rows as live

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups every CalendarCache row for the credential and returns max(updatedAt), with no expiresAt >= now() filter. getCachedAvailability in the same repository only serves rows that have not expired, so the settings dropdown can show a last-updated time and a delete action for cache that availability lookups will ignore. The new migration also backfills updatedAt to NOW() for every existing row, including expired ones, so right after deploy those stale rows look freshly updated. Filter to non-expired rows (and treat no matching row as no cache) so the status matches what is actually served.

Deleting cache does not refresh cache status

deleteCache.useMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. It never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component which invalidates that query in onSettled. cacheUpdatedAt comes from that query, and SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper loads it with refetchOnWindowFocus: false. After a successful delete the dropdown still shows the old timestamp and the delete action, so the UI claims cache exists when the rows are gone. onChanged is optional and is not guaranteed to refetch this query, so the mutation itself needs to invalidate connectedCalendars.

dev:cron now depends on undeclared npx tsx

dev:cron was changed from ts-node (declared in this package's devDependencies) to npx tsx, but tsx is not a dependency of apps/web. Under Yarn Berry, npx does not reliably resolve workspace binaries and may download an unpinned tsx or fail offline, so yarn dev:cron can break. This change is unrelated to calendar cache and should use a declared runner instead of npx.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget after awaited deletes were removed

Cancel, reschedule, and workflow-update callers used to collect prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany promises and await them before returning. That awaited delete is gone. They now call async deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach and never await the promises: handleCancelBooking.ts around the new reminder loop, handleNewBooking.ts reschedule (the try/catch there cannot observe async failures), bookings.tsx requestReschedule, and the workflow update/delete paths in workflows.tsx. For an already-scheduled email, the cancelled=true update inside that floating call is the only signal the cron uses to withdraw the SendGrid batch. For an unscheduled email or SMS (no referenceId), the helper's row delete is the only thing stopping the reminder cron from sending it; scheduleEmailReminders schedules every scheduled=false email inside 72 hours and does not check booking status. On a serverless invocation those promises can be frozen when the handler returns, so the booking is cancelled but the reminder is still sent. The calls have to be awaited, and failures surfaced, before the handler finishes.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete still hits SendGrid and never records cancellation

deleteScheduledEmailReminder's immediateDelete branch POSTs /v3/user/scheduled_sends with status cancel and then returns without setting WorkflowReminder.cancelled and without deleting the row. Reschedule in handleNewBooking.ts (the call that passes true), workflow deletion in workflows.tsx, and workflow-step deletion in workflows.tsx all use that branch. That reintroduces the failure this PR describes: each cancel stays in SendGrid's scheduled_sends list until the original send time, and once the pending-cancellation cap (stated as 100) is reached further cancels fail and the email is still sent. Failures are only logged inside the helper, and cancelled is never set, so the new cron cannot retry. Workflow and step deletion then cascade-delete the WorkflowReminder, which also removes any chance of a later retry; a bulk delete of more than 100 already-scheduled reminders therefore silently leaves the overflow emails queued. On reschedule the old booking is not deleted, so the row stays scheduled=true and cancelled=null: if the SendGrid call failed the old reminder is still delivered, and if it succeeded the stale row is only removed when scheduledDate passes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cron deletes due reminders before withdrawing them from SendGrid

scheduleEmailReminders begins by deleteMany-ing every EMAIL WorkflowReminder whose scheduledDate is at or before now, and only afterward loads cancelled=true rows to POST a SendGrid cancel. Any cancelled reminder whose send time has already arrived is removed from the database and never cancelled at SendGrid, so the email is still delivered. With the job running every 15 minutes, a cancellation made after the last tick before scheduledDate (or any run that starts at or after the send time, including a delayed cron) always hits this path. The new cancel query cannot see those rows because they are already gone. SendGrid withdrawal for cancelled=true reminders has to run before this cleanup, and the cleanup must not delete cancelled rows that have not yet been cancelled at SendGrid.

No regression test for deferred cancellation of scheduled reminders

The description says the previous SendGrid cancel fix did not work in production, but this change adds no test for the replacement contract. Nothing asserts that booking cancel sets WorkflowReminder.cancelled instead of POSTing scheduled_sends immediately, that reschedule does not use the immediate SendGrid cancel, that the cron withdraws cancelled batches before deleting past-due rows, or that one failed cancel is retried without dropping the rest of the batch. Those are the paths that still send reminders for cancelled and rescheduled bookings, and they will regress silently without a test.

One SendGrid cancel error aborts the batch and drops successful deletes

The new cancel loop awaits every SendGrid POST inside a single try/catch, and only after the whole loop does it await the queued workflowReminder.delete calls. Prisma queries are lazy, so those deletes have not run yet. If any request throws (unknown or already-cancelled batch id, the pending-cancellation cap, a network error), the catch only logs and then the handler goes on to schedule other mail. None of the reminders already cancelled at SendGrid are deleted, and every reminder after the failure is skipped. Those rows stay cancelled=true and are retried on the next run. There is no orderBy and no per-item isolation, so one permanently failing row can be selected first every 15 minutes and block every other cancellation until scheduledDate passes. At that point the opening deleteMany removes the rows without a SendGrid cancel and the emails send. Each reminder needs its own error handling, and a successful cancel must be persisted immediately so it is not retried and cannot poison the queue.

Paid cancellations return before workflow reminders are cancelled

In handleCancelBooking a paid booking is refunded and then returns 'Booking successfully cancelled' before the new reminder-cancellation loop. The booking status is already CANCELLED or REJECTED, but its WorkflowReminder rows are left untouched. Before/after-event workflow emails and SMS for paid bookings are therefore neither marked cancelled, deleted, nor withdrawn from SendGrid/Twilio, which is the same production failure this PR is fixing. The cancellation loop has to run on this path as well, and be awaited, before the early return.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Vital reschedule drops calendar and video cleanup

Reschedule now awaits the async getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). Array.forEach never waits for async callbacks and discards their return values, so the try/catch around the loop cannot see failures. getCalendar suspends on a dynamic app import before calendar.deleteEvent is called, and the video branch only returns deleteMeeting, which itself now awaits getVideoAdapters before calling the provider. Nothing awaits those floating promises. The function then sends the reschedule email and returns true. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was at least issued before the function continued. After this change a serverless worker can finish the request and freeze before the import resumes, so the cancelled booking's calendar event and video meeting are never removed (the slot stays busy and attendees still see the old event). Rejections become unhandled promise rejections. Await the references with for...of or Promise.all, including both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting, before sending email.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring cancel never joins calendar deletions

Cancelling all remaining instances of a recurring booking deletes external calendar events with credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(await calendar.deleteEvent(...)) }). forEach does not return those promises, and the push onto apiDeletes happens only after deleteEvent has already resolved, so the later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) neither starts nor waits for this work. This change made getCalendar async (it now awaits a dynamic import) while leaving this loop in place; the non-recurring branch just below was correctly rewritten as a for...of that awaits getCalendar and pushes the in-flight deleteEvent promise. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was invoked before the callback's first await and the provider request was at least started. Now the callback suspends before deleteEvent is issued. The handler can mark the series CANCELLED, send the cancellation email, and return while those events are still on the external calendar; on serverless the continuations are often dropped. Failures are unhandled rejections. Replace the forEach with a for...of or Promise.all and include each deleteEvent promise in apiDeletes before awaiting them.

WipeMyCal reschedule drops calendar and video cleanup

The WipeMyCal reschedule handler awaits getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach does not await async callbacks and ignores what they return, so the surrounding try/catch never handles rejections. Because app modules are now dynamic imports, getCalendar yields before calendar.deleteEvent runs, and the video branch returns deleteMeeting without awaiting it even though deleteMeeting now waits on getVideoAdapters before deleting the meeting. The handler proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns true while that work is still suspended. Before this change getCalendar was sync, so the calendar delete was started before the function moved on. On serverless the process can exit when the handler returns, leaving the old calendar event and video room in place after the booking is marked cancelled. Use for...of or Promise.all and await both provider deletes before sending email.

requestReschedule does not wait for provider cancellation

requestReschedule awaits getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach does not join those promises, so the mutation continues, sends the reschedule email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and resolves while calendar deletion is still suspended on the app-store dynamic import. The video branch only returns deleteMeeting from that callback; deleteMeeting now awaits getVideoAdapters before it calls the provider, so that cleanup is deferred the same way and is also not awaited. The booking row is already set to CANCELLED before this loop. If the worker stops when the tRPC mutation returns, which is typical on serverless, the provider calls never run and the old calendar event and video room remain. There is no try/catch around the loop, so a rejection is unhandled rather than a failed mutation. Await the references with for...of or Promise.all, including deleteEvent and deleteMeeting, before email or webhooks.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours gate frees non-working days and drops split shifts

The new working-hours check uses find() to look for a same-day window that does not contain the slot, and treats "no such window" as available. If a fixed host has no entry for that weekday, every callback is falsy, find returns undefined, and the slot is kept. That is the round-robin case this PR is meant to close: union slots from a rotating host stay bookable on days the fixed host does not work. The same predicate rejects valid slots when a host has two windows on one day (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00): the window that does not contain the slot makes find succeed and the slot is removed, so lunch-break schedules disappear from the booking page for every fixed host, not only round-robin. end is also copied from slotStartTime (line 142) instead of slotEndTime, so a slot that starts inside the window but runs past endTime is still treated as inside. A single window that fully contains the slot start still passes, which is why the existing one-range tests do not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Override window test misses blocked days, partial overlaps, and extra ranges

A full-day block is stored as an override whose start equals its end, and this callback tries to reject the whole day in that case. The comparison uses === on two dayjs objects, which is reference equality and is never true, so that branch never runs. The following checks only mark a slot outside a window when the slot ends at or before the override start or starts strictly after the override end. A slot that merely overlaps the window — starts before it, ends after it, or straddles a zero-length block — is treated as inside. find() then stops at the first same-day range that does not contain the slot, so two override ranges on one day (a normal custom-hours override with a gap) reject a slot that sits inside the other range and the day shows no bookable override slots. The date match also uses only the adjusted start, so an override whose UTC interval crosses midnight does not cover slots on the second day. After a timezone shift, a midnight–midnight block can land on the previous UTC date and miss the intended day entirely, leaving a fixed host bookable on a day they marked unavailable.

false_positives.candidate:
Already-adjusted override minutes are DST-shifted again in buildSlots

The new override minutes are computed from the override date's own organizer and invitee offsets, so they are already invitee-local minutes for that date. They are then pushed into computedLocalAvailability and passed through buildSlots, which adds organizerDSTDiff - inviteeDSTDiff. That correction exists for working hours converted with today's offset (dayjs.tz(dayjs(), timeZone)), not for values already adjusted to the target date. When today and the booking day sit on different sides of a DST transition and the invitee timezone does not have the same delta, override slots move by an hour. Asia/Kolkata and Asia/Dhaka do not observe DST, so the added test cannot see it.

Override date match compares server-local date to UTC date

Whether an override applies to a slot is decided by formatting the offset-adjusted start with a local-mode dayjs and comparing it to slotStartTime.format(), and slotStartTime is in UTC mode (time.utc()). format() on a local-mode instance uses the process timezone, not UTC. Whenever the server timezone is not UTC, the two calendar dates disagree for overrides near midnight and the override is applied to the wrong day or not applied at all, so fixed-host date overrides silently fail outside a UTC process.

Slots inside a date override skip busy checks and can double-book

checkIfIsAvailable now returns true as soon as a slot falls on a day with a date override and is treated as inside that override, before the busy-interval scan. That scan is the only place calendar conflicts and existing Cal bookings are applied to generated slots, and this function now runs for every fixed host — including ordinary personal and collective events, whose users are marked isFixed. On any day that has a date override, a slot inside the override is therefore shown as free even when the host is already booked, so the same time can be booked twice.

Tests never exercise fixed-host overrides or a real timezone day shift

The only new assertion re-requests the existing personal-event IST override in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants. That is a 30-minute shift that stays inside one calendar day and never hits checkIfIsAvailable's fixed-host path with a host who is actually isFixed. Nothing covers a round-robin event with a fixed host whose date override or weekday hours are narrower than the rotating host, a blocked day (start equal to end), a booking or calendar conflict on an override day, split windows, or an override that crosses midnight after timezone conversion. The scenario helper also never attaches eventType.hosts as {isFixed, user}, so the existing round-robin tests leave every user isFixed false and would not exercise this gate even if a case were added. The regressions above can merge green.

Timezone-adjusted overrides drop the day and can wipe that day's hours

Override start/end are converted by adding the invitee-minus-organizer offset and then keeping only hour and minute. That throws away a day boundary. If the shift moves one end across midnight and not the other, endTime is less than startTime; buildSlots discards any range with start >= end. The caller has already deleted that user's normal working hours for the invitee day the raw UTC timestamp fell on, so the day is left with no slots. Even when both ends wrap to clock times on the same side of midnight, the activeOverrides filter (line 206) still selects the invitee day that contains the unadjusted timestamp, whose UTC clock is the organizer wall time rather than the real instant. For a non-zero organizer offset those are different instants, so an evening override viewed from a timezone ahead (US host, European booker) is attached to the wrong calendar day. The new +6 test only shifts IST 14:00–18:00 by 30 minutes and stays on the same day, so it does not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth state is not unique per install attempt

OAuthLoginView sets the OAuth state query parameter to pipeline.signature (integration.py line 402) and later accepts the callback when that value matches (line 412). The new tests require this state to be exactly 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 for every fresh pipeline, including organization_2's pipeline in test_github_installed_on_another_org, which only reaches the "installed on another Sentry organization" error after the state check. So the value is not a per-flow nonce. PipelineAdvancerView has csrf_protect = False and auth_required = False, and the callback is a GET, so a top-level navigation still sends the session cookie under SameSite=Lax. Any user can start an install, copy state from their own authorize redirect, and send a victim who has an in-progress pipeline to /extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker code>&state=<that value>&installation_id=<attacker installation>. The callback is accepted, github_authenticated_user becomes the attacker, and the sender check then passes because both sides are the attacker, linking the attacker's GitHub App installation to the victim's Sentry organization.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Installer check crashes when sender login is missing

When an ACTIVE Integration exists but has no OrganizationIntegration, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] (integration.py lines 501-504) with no existence check. build_integration only writes metadata["sender"] if state already contains sender, and test_basic_flow expects a pipeline-created integration to have no sender key at all. Hitting this branch for a row without that nested login (pipeline-created integration, older webhook data, or sender stored as a string) raises KeyError or TypeError. The user gets a 500 instead of the installation-failed dialog, and the security comparison never runs. A missing sender should fail closed through error().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Installer identity check is skipped for new installations

GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() as soon as Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist (integration.py around line 481). That is the normal install path: assert_setup_flow never creates a webhook Integration and still finishes successfully. It is also the race where GitHub's setup redirect arrives before the installation webhook. build_integration only reads installation_id (and optional sender); it never reads github_authenticated_user, so the OAuth login collected by OAuthLoginView is discarded. Linking then uses the GitHub App's own credentials. Anyone who knows a Sentry GitHub App installation_id (it is in the post-install redirect and in GitHub's installation settings URL) can attach that installation to their Sentry organization before an Integration row exists. After that, the real installer hits the existing "installed on another Sentry organization" error and is locked out. The new sender comparison only runs later, and only when an ACTIVE Integration already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration.

New security checks are not actually asserted

test_installation_not_found still stubs the installation API as 404, but the follow-up request uses state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature the other tests use (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3). OAuthLoginView rejects that state and returns the generic invalid-installation page before build_integration or the 404 path runs. The assertion was changed from "The GitHub installation could not be found." to "Invalid installation request.", so the test stays green if 404 handling is removed. test_github_user_mismatch has the same blind spot: it only asserts that generic string, which is also what state mismatch and token failure return, so it does not prove the sender comparison ran. That test also changes installation id and sender.login on INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE but keeps the original X-Hub-Signature (test_integration.py line 423). If webhook signature verification is enabled, the webhook is rejected and no Integration with sender "attacker" is created, so the mismatch path is never set up.

Token exchange omits redirect_uri sent at authorize

The authorize redirect always includes redirect_uri (integration.py lines 404-408), but the access-token POST (lines 416-423) sends only code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, and OAuth 2.0 RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, require the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in the authorization request; otherwise GitHub returns an error and no access_token. This code treats a missing access_token as a failed install and shows "Invalid installation request." The new tests stub https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token to always return a token, so they never observe the rejection. The authorize URL is also built with string interpolation instead of urlencode, so redirect_uri is not percent-encoded and can fail to match a properly encoded value. Because every GitHub install now goes through this step, token exchange can fail for all users once it is live.

installation_id is stored before the callback is authenticated

OAuthLoginView copies request.GET installation_id into pipeline state (integration.py lines 397-399) before it checks state or exchanges the code. A request that only has installation_id still performs that write and then redirects to GitHub OAuth because state is missing (line 401). GitHub's OAuth callback does not include installation_id, so it will not clear the poisoned value. GitHubInstallation also prefers a query-string installation_id over the saved one (lines 448-450). The setup endpoint is an unauthenticated GET with CSRF disabled, so a user who already has an install pipeline and opens .../extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<id> gets that id attached to their session. After they complete the OAuth step, the pipeline links that substituted installation. Together with the branch that skips the installer check when no Integration row exists, a malicious link during install attaches the attacker's GitHub App installation to the victim's Sentry organization.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is fixed at import time

AssignmentSource.queued is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. Dataclass defaults are evaluated once when the class body runs, not when each instance is created, and datetime is immutable so this does not raise the mutable-default error. Every AssignmentSource built by from_integration (the inbound webhook path) or by from_dict when queued is omitted therefore shares one timestamp: the moment this module was imported in that process, not when the assignment was queued. to_dict()/asdict() copies that stale value into the Celery kwargs for sync_assignee_outbound, so task payloads carry a misleading queue time. The cycle check does not read queued today, but the field cannot be used to order or drop the rapid assignee updates this change is about, and debugging those races from the payload will be wrong. tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py only asserts queued is not None, so it does not catch this. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now). Also, to_dict() emits the raw datetime and from_dict() will not parse an ISO string back into a datetime, so the dict is only safe if the task serializer preserves datetime objects.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
