true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: backup code validation using `indexOf` is case-sensitive, causing validation to fail if the user inputs uppercase hex characters instead of lowercase.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

After a backup code matches, the handler nulls that array slot and writes the re-encrypted list with a plain read-modify-write. The user row is not locked and the write is not conditional on the ciphertext that was just read. Two overlapping logins with the same code both see it as unused and both get a session, so the code is not single-use. Two overlapping logins with different codes can also lose an update: each write is based on a stale list, and the last write puts the other code back. Consume the code in a transaction that locks the user row, or compare-and-swap on the previous ciphertext, and only then issue the session.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same race condition where backup codes are read, modified in memory, and written back non-atomically, allowing concurrent login requests to reuse the same single-use backup code.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code alone can log in if any TOTP value is also sent

The new backup-code branch in credentials authorize never checks the primary factor. Password verification only runs when credentials.totpCode is empty, and non-CAL users are rejected only when totpCode is empty. A caller who knows the email and one backup code can sign in by posting any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000") with that backup code and a wrong or empty password. The password check and the identity-provider check are both skipped, and a matching backup code creates a session. A backup code then replaces the password or the IdP login, not only the authenticator, which contradicts the UI copy. The disable endpoint does not have this hole: it verifies the CAL password before accepting a backup code. This branch must verify the primary factor even when totpCode is present, and a non-CAL account must not be able to finish credentials login with only a backup code.

Dismissing the backup-code step skips onEnable and loses the codes

A successful TOTP enable used to call onEnable() immediately. It now only moves to the backup-code step, and onEnable() runs only from the Close button. The dialog still takes onOpenChange, so Escape, the overlay, or the X control closes it without onEnable() or resetState(). Two-factor is already enabled on the server, but the parent is not notified, so the settings switch stays off and a later toggle tries to enable again and fails as already enabled. The codes live only in this component's state, are never shown again, and there is no regenerate action, so that dismiss also permanently drops the only copy. A refresh on this step has the same result. Block dismissal until the user finishes, or treat every close of this step as completion and call onEnable().

Download control nests a button in an anchor inside the enable form

The download control is a Button wrapped in an anchor with the blob URL, inside the form whose submit handler is handleEnable. Interactive content inside an anchor is invalid HTML, and browsers often do not follow the link when the click target is a button, so Download can save nothing. The button also does not set type="button". The copy and close buttons in this footer call preventDefault because a click submits the form; this control cannot do that without also cancelling the download. A click can therefore POST /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable again after 2FA is already on, while the file may not download. Use a type="button" control that starts the blob download without wrapping a button in an anchor.

Lost-access button also submits the disable form

The new Lost access / Go back button is inside the disable Form and neither sets type="button" nor calls preventDefault. The real disable control in the same footer is type="submit", and the enable modal's non-submit actions call preventDefault because clicks in these forms submit. Clicking Lost access therefore also runs handleDisable. The click handler clears the code fields first, so the request is sent with an empty TOTP and backup code, the API returns a second-factor or incorrect-code error, and that error is shown just for switching modes. This disable path is untested. Set type="button" on the toggle.

Backup-code auth is untested and the enable assertion cannot fail

The enable-and-login test never closes the new backup-code step, so onEnable() does not run and the switch is not updated. It then asserts expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy(). isChecked() returns a Promise, and a Promise object is always truthy, so the assertion passes without 2FA being enabled. The test can also log out before the enable request finishes. The new steps only check that a download is named cal-backup-codes.txt and that a success toast appears; they do not read the file or use a code. Nothing covers login with a backup code, single-use consumption, a password-less backup-code attempt, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. Those are the paths with the auth and race bugs.

Copy toast fires before the clipboard write succeeds

The copy handler calls navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting or catching it, then immediately shows a success toast. writeText rejects when permission is denied or the clipboard API is missing. The user is told the codes were copied, closes the dialog, and cannot view them again. Await the write and toast only on success; show an error if it fails.

Empty backup-code submit shows no error

The login form sets noValidate, and the zod schema only validates email and password before passthrough, so the BackupCode required and minLength attributes are not enforced. Submitting Lost access with an empty code sends a falsy backupCode. The server treats that as not using a backup code, requires a TOTP code, and returns SecondFactorRequired. This handler only sets twoFactorRequired and does not set an error, so the submit looks like it did nothing. Validate backupCode on that step and show an error for an empty submission.

Missing-backup-codes text points at a settings action that does not exist

missing_backup_codes says to generate codes in settings. Users who enabled 2FA before this column existed, and anyone with null backupCodes, see this on login and when disabling 2FA. There is no settings action to generate codes while 2FA is already on: setup returns two-factor-already-enabled, and codes are only created during enable. The instruction cannot be followed. Tell them to disable and re-enable 2FA with the authenticator, or add a real regenerate action and then point at it.

If the list is null, undefined, or [] (the value many callers now pass when nobody has a destination calendar), destructuring yields undefined and this throws TypeError before any video or calendar work. Previously optional chaining treated a missing calendar as not Google and replaced Meet with integrations:daily. Any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar, including confirmation and payment flows that pass [], now fails the whole create instead of falling back to Cal Video.

Video references no longer store credentialId

referencesToCreate used to persist result.credentialId for non-calendar results and now stores undefined whenever the result is not a calendar type. updateLocation in this same file still copies result.credentialId, so this is an accidental drop. handleCancelBooking only calls deleteMeeting when the video BookingReference has a credentialId, and there is no fallback lookup by integration type. New bookings will therefore not record the video credential, and cancelling them leaves the Zoom, Daily, or other video room in place.

If neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, the field is null and the push is a no-op, so every other host is discarded. createAllCalendarEvents then falls back to credentials whose type is exactly "calendar", which never matches google_calendar, office365_calendar, and the rest, so nobody gets a calendar event. Booking.destinationCalendar is a single relation and the create payload connects only evt.destinationCalendar[0]. The other hosts' calendars exist only on the in-memory event used for the immediate create. Stripe payment_intent.succeeded and setup_intent.succeeded, and PayPal handlePaymentSuccess, rebuild CalendarEvent from that one booking or user record and call EventManager.create. confirm.handler does the same and passes the evt to handleConfirmation. Collective bookings whose calendar events are created after payment or after organizer approval therefore only write the first calendar; every other host is skipped even if the initial assembly was correct.

The non-recurring branch deletes each calendar reference with that reference's credential. The all-remaining recurring branch was not updated: it still loads only the booking owner's calendar credentials and, for each instance, uses find() so only the first _calendar reference is deleted. It is also nested inside the new per-reference loop, so that incomplete deletion runs once per calendar reference. Other hosts' credentials are never loaded, Google 404s from the wrong token are treated as success, and the booking is already marked cancelled. createEvent selects the calendar only by matching destinationCalendar.credentialId to the credential used for the call. When a seated booking is moved onto an existing slot, every other host's old calendar event is left in place at the original time. Consumers that read payload.destinationCalendar.externalId or .integration will now see an array (or crash). The PR is marked non-breaking, but this is a public payload change. true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Vital reschedule drops calendar and video cleanup

Reschedule now awaits the async getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). Array.forEach never waits for async callbacks and discards their return values, so the try/catch around the loop cannot see failures. getCalendar suspends on a dynamic app import before calendar.deleteEvent is called, and the video branch only returns deleteMeeting, which itself now awaits getVideoAdapters before calling the provider. Nothing awaits those floating promises. The function then sends the reschedule email and returns true. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was at least issued before the function continued. After this change a serverless worker can finish the request and freeze before the import resumes, so the cancelled booking's calendar event and video meeting are never removed (the slot stays busy and attendees still see the old event). Rejections become unhandled promise rejections. Await the references with for...of or Promise.all, including both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting, before sending email.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: using `Array.forEach` with an `async` callback for calendar/video event cleanup results in unawaited promises, leading to incomplete cleanup and unhandled promise rejections that bypass surrounding try/catch blocks. Both suggest replacing `forEach` with `for...of` or `Promise.all`.

false_positives.candidate:
WipeMyCal reschedule drops calendar and video cleanup

The WipeMyCal reschedule handler awaits getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach does not await async callbacks and ignores what they return, so the surrounding try/catch never handles rejections. Because app modules are now dynamic imports, getCalendar yields before calendar.deleteEvent runs, and the video branch returns deleteMeeting without awaiting it even though deleteMeeting now waits on getVideoAdapters before deleting the meeting. The handler proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns true while that work is still suspended. Before this change getCalendar was sync, so the calendar delete was started before the function moved on. On serverless the process can exit when the handler returns, leaving the old calendar event and video room in place after the booking is marked cancelled. Use for...of or Promise.all and await both provider deletes before sending email.

requestReschedule does not wait for provider cancellation

requestReschedule awaits getCalendar inside bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach does not join those promises, so the mutation continues, sends the reschedule email and BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and resolves while calendar deletion is still suspended on the app-store dynamic import. The video branch only returns deleteMeeting from that callback; deleteMeeting now awaits getVideoAdapters before it calls the provider, so that cleanup is deferred the same way and is also not awaited. The booking row is already set to CANCELLED before this loop. If the worker stops when the tRPC mutation returns, which is typical on serverless, the provider calls never run and the old calendar event and video room remain. There is no try/catch around the loop, so a rejection is unhandled rather than a failed mutation. Await the references with for...of or Promise.all, including deleteEvent and deleteMeeting, before email or webhooks.

Recurring cancel never joins calendar deletions

Cancelling all remaining instances of a recurring booking deletes external calendar events with credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(await calendar.deleteEvent(...)) }). forEach does not return those promises, and the push onto apiDeletes happens only after deleteEvent has already resolved, so the later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) neither starts nor waits for this work. This change made getCalendar async (it now awaits a dynamic import) while leaving this loop in place; the non-recurring branch just below was correctly rewritten as a for...of that awaits getCalendar and pushes the in-flight deleteEvent promise. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was invoked before the callback's first await and the provider request was at least started. Now the callback suspends before deleteEvent is issued. The handler can mark the series CANCELLED, send the cancellation email, and return while those events are still on the external calendar; on serverless the continuations are often dropped. Failures are unhandled rejections. Replace the forEach with a for...of or Promise.all and include each deleteEvent promise in apiDeletes before awaiting them.

spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce is recorded with tag key "shards", while spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes in the same loop use "shard". Anything filtering or grouping the flusher timers by shard silently drops produce-ack wait time, so latency dashboards under-report the time spent blocked on Kafka and make the flusher look healthier than it is.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Drift wait in test_basic is a no-op, so the flush assertion is racy

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then after setting current_drift to 9000 calls time.sleep(0.1) with a comment that it gives the flusher time to run. That sleep is the patched no-op, so it does not wait. step.join() then sets the shared stopped flag immediately, and the flusher only produces inside `while not stopped`. If the flusher thread does not get the GIL between the drift write and that flag, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. The same patch turns SpanFlusher.join's time.sleep(0.1) into a GIL-holding busy spin, so whether the test passes depends on accidental thread switches. The sleep added in this PR does not close the race it was meant to fix.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting to give the flusher time to run. Its additional race-condition explanation elaborates on the consequence of that ineffective wait.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Replacing a flusher does not wait for the old one to stop

When a flusher is dead or hung, _ensure_processes_alive kill()s it and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards, without join()ing the old process. kill()/os.kill returns when the signal is queued, not when the process has exited; a process blocked in a syscall keeps running until the call returns, and SIGKILL does not cancel an in-flight Redis flush or Kafka produce. The old Process is then overwritten in self.processes, so nothing ever waits for it. The replacement starts flush_segments on the same shards while the old process may already have produced those segments and not yet called done_flush_segments, so the same segment is written to buffered-segments twice (or a partial delete races the new read). The kill is also skipped for threading.Thread (the produce_to_pipe path) because it is guarded by isinstance(..., multiprocessing.Process), and that check does not match the spawn-context process type this file annotates as multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess if that class is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process — in that case a hung production flusher is never killed and a second flusher is started beside it. A slow produce that exceeds spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds takes this path, not only hard crashes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the multiprocessing.Process isinstance guard does not match spawn-context SpawnProcess instances, causing hung flushers to remain alive while replacements start. This matches the golden issue, despite the candidate also discussing a separate missing-join concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shutdown abandons flusher processes once the join deadline passes

SpanFlusher.join() is the only place that stops background flushers (close() deliberately leaves them running through rebalance). It spends the entire caller timeout in next_step.join(timeout) first, then walks self.processes and breaks as soon as the deadline is already past. That break skips both the wait and process.terminate() for the current process and every process after it. With the old single-process join, terminate() always ran after the wait; this loop does not. If CommitOffsets.join consumes the timeout, or one slow flusher uses up what remains, the other flushers are left alive. They are daemons, so they keep calling flush_segments and producing to buffered-segments while the consumer process stays up. Rebalance then builds a new SpanFlusher for the same partitions, and the old and new flushers flush the same Redis shards and emit duplicate segments. Even the path that does call terminate() never join()s the child, so join() can return while a just-signaled process is still producing. Under load — the case this change is meant to handle — a flush/produce longer than the join timeout is exactly when this fires.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: breaking out of the shutdown loop after the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running. The candidate adds consequences and related concerns but clearly captures the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Flusher metric shard tag is a comma-separated list

Each flusher process sets shard_tag to ",".join of every shard it owns and puts that string on spans.buffer.flusher.produce, spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes, and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce. The new --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, so the default production setup runs one process for every assigned partition and the tag value is the full partition list (for example "0,1,2,5"), not a single shard. StatsD/DogStatsD frames tags as a comma-separated list, so shard:0,1,2 is parsed as shard=0 plus stray tags, the series cannot be grouped by shard, and the value changes on every rebalance (new cardinality). A long assignment can also exceed backend tag-length limits. The unhealthy metric already emits one integer shard tag per shard; these timers should do the same, or use a process index that does not contain commas.

flusher_processes of 0 or negative does not do what the flag says

--flusher-processes is an unconstrained click int, and SpanFlusher sets max_processes with `max_processes or len(assigned_shards)`. 0 is falsy, so --flusher-processes 0 does not cap the flusher; it spawns one process per assigned shard. Each of those is a spawn-context process that imports the full Sentry app, so a config template that sets 0 (meaning unset or disabled) can start dozens of Django processes and OOM the pod. A negative value is truthy, then min(negative, shard_count) is negative, range() is empty, and no flusher process is created. self.buffers and process_backpressure_since are then empty, so neither Redis-memory hard backpressure nor flusher backpressure can fire, and the consumer keeps writing spans to Redis and never flushes them. The option needs a minimum of 1, and 0 must not be coerced into one-process-per-shard.

No test flushes spans across multiple flusher processes

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts that four partitions yield two thread objects and that the shard lists sum to 4. It never submits a span or checks that each shard is flushed once. Every flush test passes produce_to_pipe, which forces threading.Thread instead of a spawn-context Process, so the production path — per-process KafkaProducer, kill/restart, and join/terminate — never runs. A bad shard split, a double-flush on restart, or the join timeout leak would not fail CI.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Report validation rejects real browser URLs and ignores age 0

`url` is a DRF `URLField`, which only allows http(s)/ftp(s). Reporting API document URLs are often `about:blank`, `chrome-extension:`, or other non-http schemes. Those reports now 422 the entire batch; the previous dataclass accepted any string. `validate_timestamp` / `validate_age` also use `initial_data.get("age")` and `get("timestamp")`, which are falsy for 0, so a spec-valid `age: 0` combined with a timestamp skips the mutual-exclusion error (and the reverse). Allow the schemes browsers actually send, and test key presence rather than truthiness.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same truthiness bug: using initial_data.get('timestamp') or get('age') treats 0 as absent and bypasses mutual-exclusion validation. It also recommends checking key presence, matching the golden comment despite including an additional URL validation issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Unnormalized error timestamps crash or mis-order summaries

Error context defaults on. Timestamps from nodestore are stored raw and then compared with `<` to each segment event's numeric `timestamp` (default 0) while merging logs. Ingested events persist `timestamp` as an ISO-8601 string; `str < float` raises TypeError outside `fetch_error_details`'s try/except, so any replay with error ids 500s the summarize endpoint instead of returning a summary. The new test passes a float into `store_event`, so it does not lock the production shape. Segment fixtures in this same file use small offsets like `0.0` while event timestamps are unix time, so even two numbers will not interleave. Coerce both sides to one numeric unit before sort/compare.

Error ids depend on the client's field allowlist

The endpoint always runs `process_raw_response(..., fields=request.query_params.getlist("field"))` and then reads `error_ids` from that projection. The replay AI tab calls this URL with no `field` param, and any caller that passes `field` for something else will not include `error_ids`. If that helper only emits requested keys, error context is silently empty in the UI this change is for. The new test also omits `field` while expecting exception text in the Seer body, so it only passes if an empty field list means "all fields". Force `error_ids` into the internal lookup instead of forwarding the client field list.

Each segment page is summarized with every remaining error

`error_events` is closed over the paginator `on_results` callback, but `gen_request_data` flushes every not-yet-emitted error after the current page's segments. `GenericOffsetPaginator` only supplies one page (a long replay is many more than one page of segments). The first page, which is all the AI tab loads, therefore appends later errors instead of interleaving them with later breadcrumbs, and later pages repeat those errors in their Seer requests. Only emit errors whose timestamps fall in the page being summarized.

Unescaped issue titles break or inject PR comment links

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` puts the issue title inside a markdown link (`[**{title}**]({url})`) after only truncating to 50 characters. Titles often contain `]`. That character closes the link early, so the GitHub/GitLab suspect-issue comment points at the wrong URL. A title an attacker can set by sending an error, such as `Click me](https://evil.example)`, injects an arbitrary link into the bot comment developers read on the PR. Escape `]` (and other markdown link characters) before formatting.

Hidden span attributes are still shown until the user searches

`HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is applied only in the search branch. An empty `searchQuery` returns `sortAttributes(attributes)` immediately, so those fields remain in the default attributes panel. The hide filter has to run before that early return; otherwise the new constant never affects the view users actually see.

Feedback summary ignores the environment page filter

The summary request sends only the normalized datetime and `selection.projects`. The list page is under `PageFiltersContainer`, so the feedback list is environment-scoped, but this query never sends `selection.environments` (or the active feedback search). With an environment selected, the summary above the list describes feedback from other environments than the rows the user is looking at.

60s auth-check deadline skips SSO refresh after last_synced is bumped

`check_auth_identities` now has `processing_deadline_duration=60` and previously had none. It walks up to `chunk_size` (default 100) identities, each doing an organization RPC plus `provider.refresh_identity` HTTP. If the worker is killed at 60s, the trailing `check_auth.apply_async` that continues the chain never runs. `check_auth` already set `last_synced=now` for the whole id list before enqueue, so those identities are not selected again for about a day and their SSO validity is not refreshed. Raise the deadline to fit the batch, or set `last_synced` only after a successful check.

AI summary errors while the project list is still loading

The new guard treats `replayRecord.project_id && !project` as "Project not found". `useProjectFromId` is also undefined while the project store is still loading, not only when the id is missing. The first render shows an error alert and keeps the summarize query disabled (`project?.slug` is missing) until projects arrive, instead of the loading state. Only show that error after the project list has finished loading.

Trace waterfall wrapper lost height 100%

The waterfall root changed from a flex column with `flex-grow: 1` and `height: 100%` to `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>`. `flex={1}` does not set height. If the parent lays this view out by height rather than as a stretched flex item, the waterfall no longer fills the trace viewer and scrolling breaks. Put an explicit `height`/`min-height: 100%` back on that container.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW permission is treated as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() treats a grant of either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource as success. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires only MANAGE, and V1 canManage() only checks the manage-users role, so this is not the intended scope model. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls requireManage() before creating a group and applying its attributes, so an admin who was given only Groups VIEW can create top-level groups. The new GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() javadoc repeats the mistake (it says V2 manage is true for VIEW or MANAGE), and GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest never asserts that VIEW alone cannot create or update groups.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same scope-check bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): accepting VIEW as well as MANAGE allows users with only group VIEW permission to gain management/write access. The candidate adds supporting examples without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Member search filter uses authz resource IDs, not group IDs

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() into hasPermission() and adds that same value to the returned set. hasPermission() looks the id up with resourceStore.findByName(), but per-group resources are stored with the realm group id as the name (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and a different authorization-resource UUID as getId(). The lookup misses, falls back to the all-groups resource, and never evaluates that group's own policies. The IDs handed to UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource via session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and to getUsersCount(), are therefore not group ids. If the all-groups resource has view-members or manage-members, the filter is a nonexistent group and both search and count return nobody the admin should see. If it does not, the set stays empty: search skips the DB filter and then applies canView in memory (so the new tests pass on a tiny user set) while getUsersCount() is still called with an empty group set and returns 0, and paginated search drops members who are not in the first page of all users. The type resource named "Groups" is also included by findByType and must not be treated as a group id.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying mismatch: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and returns authorization resource IDs, while hasPermission resolves resources by names representing underlying group IDs and downstream filtering/count queries expect those group IDs. It also describes the same fallback to the all-groups resource and resulting permission and filtering failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-group resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource() creates the authorization resource for a group (name = group id) and sets scopes, but never calls setType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). init() does set the type on the all-groups resource. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers candidates only via resourceStore.findByType(..., "Groups"), so individual group resources created for group permissions are invisible to that query. User search/count then cannot be restricted to the groups whose members the admin may view, even after the resource-id vs group-id mix-up is fixed. The same omission also leaves displayName unset, so permission listings have nothing to show for these resources.

Group deletion and V1 permission APIs throw under FGAP V2

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(), isPermissionsEnabled(), and the other GroupPermissionManagement methods unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature is enabled, and MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() now returns this class. AdminPermissions.registerListener still calls groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) on every GroupRemovedEvent when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, and that publish is not caught, so deleting any group in any realm fails with 500 and rolls back while V2 is on. The same throw breaks the V1 GET/PUT group management/permissions endpoints, which still call these methods after requiring only the V1 feature. There is also no V2 cleanup of the authorization resource named with the group id, so those resources are left orphaned even if the exception is later swallowed.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not upgraded with Groups

init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, and this change adds no migration to sync the schema. Realms that enabled FGAP V2 before Groups existed keep a client that has Users/Clients but not the Groups resource or the new scopes (manage-membership, manage-members, view-members). Creating a group permission then fails because the scope does not exist. Evaluating permissions calls getResourceTypeResource(), gets null, and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() passes that null to policyStore.findByResource() (implementations call resource.getId()) and, if that returned, to resource.getScopes() — a 500 on group view/list/manage checks instead of a deny. Fresh test realms hide this because init() creates the full schema only when the client is absent.

A per-group resource hides all-groups grants

hasPermission() evaluates the all-groups resource only when findByName() returns null. As soon as any permission has created a resource named with that group id, later checks for that group evaluate only that resource's policies and never the all-groups resource. An admin with MANAGE or VIEW on all groups therefore gets 403 on a group that also has a narrower permission (for example VIEW or view-members), because the all-groups policy is not consulted. The comment in this method shows all-groups permissions are supposed to be checked explicitly; the specific-resource branch skips that. GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest never combines an all-groups permission with a per-group permission, so it does not catch the deny.

Group resources are not resolved to a display name

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users type (username, or "All users"). Group resources created by this PR use the group id as the resource name and do not set a display name, so the fallback resource.getDisplayName() is null. Permission and policy listings for the new Groups resource type therefore show a blank name instead of the group name or path, including the all-groups resource unless its display name was set elsewhere.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong method

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. That is the contract of requireManageMembership, copied onto the next method. requireManageMembers actually throws when canManageMembers is false. Callers following the javadoc will enforce group membership changes instead of member management.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission contract does not match the method

The javadoc says the method returns a Stream of groups with view permission. The signature returns Set<String>, and both the V1 and V2 implementations collect groups that grant view-members or manage-members, not the group VIEW scope. UsersResource uses that set as the UserModel.GROUPS membership filter. An implementor following the javadoc would return the wrong ids and either hide members the admin may see or prefilter user search by groups whose members they cannot view.

false_positives.candidate: Choice-format strip hides HTML from the sanitizer Before the OWASP policy runs, normalizeValue() deletes every `{n,choice,...}` subformat on `error-invalid-multivalued-size` and any key starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`, using `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` which consumes arbitrary text up to the closing brace, including tags. A translation such as `{0,choice,0#minutes|1#minute|1<reset}` is reduced to `...` and passes the checker. Those time-unit strings are MessageFormat-formatted and substituted unescaped into HTML email bodies (verification, password reset, execute-actions), so a translator can inject links or markup into official mail. The same hole exists for `error-invalid-multivalued-size`. Only the choice-format `<` limit marker should be neutralized (or the subformat text itself sanitized), and a test should cover a tag hidden inside a choice branch.

Account UI validation message switched to Java MessageFormat

This account-ui bundle is loaded by i18next, which interpolates `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, and `{{2}}`. Sibling keys in the same file still use that form (for example `error-invalid-length-too-short='{{0}}' must have minimal length of {{1}}.`). This change replaces `{{0}}`/`{{1}}`/`{{2}}` with Java MessageFormat `{0}` and a `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` plural, which i18next does not evaluate. Users who fail the multivalued-size check will see the literal string, including `{0}` and the choice pattern, with no attribute name or limits. Restore the `{{n}}` placeholders and a plain wording such as `value(s)`. The Java choice format is only valid in the server-side theme bundles.

Admin UI validation message switched to Java MessageFormat

The keycloak.v2 admin console reads this file through i18next, which only substitutes `{{0}}`/`{{1}}`/`{{2}}`. The previous value used those placeholders (`Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).`). It was rewritten to Java MessageFormat `{0}` plus `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`, which the React admin UI will not format. The multivalued-size validation error will display the raw pattern and empty placeholders instead of the attribute name and bounds. Keep the `{{n}}` form and `value(s)` here. The choice-format wording in `themes/.../theme/base/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` is the copy that MessageFormat actually evaluates.

Illegal-HTML diff reporter can throw and abort the scan

When the sanitized string differs from the original, the reporter computes a common prefix (`start`) and a common suffix (`end`) independently, then calls `substring(start, length - end)` on both strings without checking that `start + end` is within each length. If those regions overlap, `substring` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. That is a realistic sanitizer result: `test<script>test` is reduced to `test`, `start` and `end` are both 4, and `sanitized.substring(4, 0)` throws. `verify()` only catches IOException, so the RuntimeException aborts the file, the Illegal HTML message is never returned, and later keys in that file are not checked. Clamp the range or fall back to the full strings before calling substring.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId

The constructor intends to reject a null raw token id, but the fourth Objects.requireNonNull checks grantType again (already checked on the previous line) and the message falsely says rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId is stored. encodeTokenId concatenates it, and Java turns null into the literal "null", producing a jti such as onrtac:null. Every token built with a null raw id shares that jti, so revocation/replay checks keyed by token id cannot tell them apart. Require rawTokenId to be non-null.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same constructor bug: the fourth Objects.requireNonNull checks grantType again instead of rawTokenId, allowing a null rawTokenId to pass validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token id matcher uses the wrong slice and inverted logic

isAccessTokenId is supposed to require the new jti to embed the expected grant shortcut, but it does not. The wire format is six characters SSTTGG before the colon, so the grant shortcut is substring(4, 6). The matcher uses substring(3, 5) (last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant; for onrtac:... that is "ta", not "ac") and returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut, so a real match would be rejected. For every built-in shortcut the wrong slice never equals the expected value (onrtrt yields "tr", not refresh shortcut "rt"), so the check is dead code: any prefix:uuid passes expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken even if the grant shortcut is wrong. A prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of failing the assertion. Require a 6-character prefix and accept only when substring(4, 6) equals the expected shortcut.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both parts of the same bug: the grant shortcut should be extracted with substring(4, 6), and matching the expected shortcut should contribute to a true result rather than return false. Its additional observations do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing grant factories

getShortcut() was added to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI with no default method. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls it on every grant factory. A custom grant-type provider compiled against the previous interface has no such method and throws AbstractMethodError during startup, which fails deployment when that provider is installed. The javadoc also says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", but the encoder and decoder require exactly two characters; an implementation that follows the javadoc mints access-token ids the default decoder cannot parse. Add a default that returns a stable 2-character shortcut (or "na") and document the exact length.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same Javadoc mismatch: it describes shortcuts as usually three letters while actual usage is two characters, and recommends updating the documentation. Its additional compatibility concern does not negate that match.

false_positives.candidate:
First offline access tokens are labeled as online sessions

Access-token ids are encoded inside createClientAccessToken/initToken, which createTokenResponse calls on line 110 while userSession is still the online session, so the jti prefix is "on". Only after that does generateRefreshToken() create the offline user session (Keycloak keeps the same session id) and, when AuthenticationProcessor.FIRST_OFFLINE_ACCESS is set, line 120 deletes the online session — before the token is signed in build() and returned. By the time the client uses the access token, that session id exists only in the offline store, but the prefix says online. ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType has the same ordering: generateAccessToken() at line 139 runs before line 145 removes the online session whenever the refresh token is offline (not only the first issuance). This prefix is meant to skip the online-then-offline session lookup. Trusting "on" for these tokens misses the session and rejects valid access tokens from offline login. Resolve the final session store before encoding the id (or rewrite the id before signing).

Grant shortcuts are not checked against the fixed 2-character format

Encoded access-token ids are session(2)+tokenType(2)+grant(2)+':'+rawId, and getTokenContextFromTokenId throws if the prefix length is not 6. postInit stores OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() with no check that it is non-null, exactly two characters, free of ':', and unique. A shortcut of any other length (including the 3-letter form described on getShortcut) is accepted, encodeTokenId embeds it, and decoding later throws IllegalArgumentException, so those tokens cannot be interpreted. A null shortcut NPEs in ConcurrentHashMap.put during postInit and aborts startup with an unclear error. The lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType (around line 112) and getGrantTypeByShortcut (around line 130) also overwrites an existing shortcut without re-running the duplicate size check, so a newly deployed grant can steal another grant's shortcut and make already-issued tokens decode as the wrong grant. Validate length, charset, and uniqueness both at startup and on the lazy path, and name the conflicting grant ids in the error.

Public Context copy constructor was deleted

The line that captures grantType from form params replaced the public OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) copy constructor instead of being added inside the primary constructor. That copy constructor is part of the grant SPI context type. Callers that clone a context with new OAuth2GrantType.Context(existing) no longer compile, including any in-repo use that this edit did not update. The deletion looks accidental. Restore the copy constructor and copy grantType as well; a clone that leaves grantType null causes access tokens to be encoded with grant shortcut "na" even when the original request had a grant. The new formParams.getFirst call also NPEs if formParams is null, which the previous constructor accepted.

Legacy token exchange still encodes grant type as unknown

The grant shortcut is taken from ClientSessionContext attribute Constants.GRANT_TYPE; if it was never set, the id is encoded with "na". Token exchange does not go through OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, so each provider must set the attribute itself. Only StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient does so (line 237). TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory still enables the legacy TOKEN_EXCHANGE feature as well as the v2 features, and the legacy V1 token-exchange provider builds access tokens in its own exchangeClientToOIDCClient path, which this PR does not change. Those tokens get grant shortcut "na" and cannot be distinguished from tokens whose grant was never recorded, so the token-exchange use case this PR is for will not see them. Any other TokenExchangeProvider that overrides exchangeClientToOIDCClient and does not call this method has the same gap. Set the attribute on the shared issuance path, not only in the standard v2 provider.

Bad token-id error claims the whole id must be length 6

When the prefix before ':' is not 6 characters, getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException saying the token id has 'Expected length of 6.' The check is only on that prefix. A valid encoded id is 6 prefix characters, a colon, and a 36-character UUID (43 characters). The message points operators at a 6-character jti and does not say which part failed. State that the context prefix before ':' must be exactly 6 characters.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials drops id and resets usage

getCredentials does not return the stored recovery-code CredentialModel. On every read it deserializes the original plaintext list and passes it to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, which builds a new all-unused model and does not keep the id assigned in updateCredential (recoveryCodesModel.setId). The id Keycloak sees is therefore null, so account-console deletion and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target the stored credential. The next-code number shown by RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean is always the first code, even after a code has been used, and any usage state a correct isValid would persist is discarded on the next read. Login keeps prompting for code 0.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that recreating RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel loses the stored credential ID, leaving getId() null and preventing removal by ID. This matches the golden issue, despite additional claims about usage state.

false_positives.candidate:
User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not sequential

BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid accepts a recovery code if any stored code equals the submitted value, and it never removes the matched code. After CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the codes in user storage, login calls credentialManager().isValid, which hits this method instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (the component that consumes a locally stored code). Nothing in the authenticator updates the stored list afterward. A previously used code therefore keeps working forever, and any of the twelve codes is accepted regardless of the index RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean displays. Shoulder-surfing or replay of one code is enough to authenticate again. The new login test only submits the first code once, so it does not catch this.

Recovery codes stored in plaintext

updateCredential saves input.getChallengeResponse() straight into CredentialModel.credentialData. That value is the JSON array of raw recovery codes written by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, and isValid later compares those strings with String.equals. The password branch in the same method hashes the secret with PasswordHashProvider before storing it. Recovery codes are password-equivalent; anyone who can read this provider's user map, or a storage implementation that persists the challenge response the same way, can log in as the user. Hash the codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode, or the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel secret format) before persisting them, and compare hashes on validation.

Recovery codes cannot be disabled

disableCredentialType only clears OTP. For recovery-authn-codes it logs that the type is unsupported and leaves MyUser.recoveryCodes set. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream likewise only reports OTP, so the admin API and account console will not treat recovery codes as disableable. OTP removal in this class works because both methods handle OTP; recovery codes need the same treatment. After setup, a user cannot turn recovery codes off, isConfiguredFor stays true, and a browser flow that requires them keeps challenging for a code that cannot be removed.

Exhausted user-storage recovery codes are not deleted

After a successful recovery-code login the authenticator now loads the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers user storage, and if allCodesUsed() is true it calls removeStoredCredentialById and ignores the result. That API deletes a row in Keycloak's local credential store. A credential created when user storage's updateCredential returns true is not in that store. The model getCredentials returns also has a null id, because createFromValues does not preserve the id stored on the provider, so the remove call cannot match the federated credential either. The exhausted credential stays configured. The next login still runs this authenticator, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() with no remaining code, which throws and fails login with a server error instead of the reconfigure required action. Cleanup needs disableCredentialType (and the storage provider must honor it); removeStoredCredentialById alone does not clear user storage.

Old local recovery codes survive user-storage create

When user.credentialManager().updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential logs success and does not delete recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local store. Before this change, federated users always received local recovery codes, because user storage did not accept the type. After this change, a provider that returns true (including BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, which newly supports the type) stores the new set externally and leaves the previous local set in place. credentialManager().isValid still tries local credential providers when the user-storage check does not accept the submitted code, so the old codes remain valid after the user generates a new set. Regeneration does not revoke previously issued recovery codes. On a successful user-storage write, existing local credentials of this type must be removed.

Recovery-code storage test misses reuse and removal

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin writes recovery codes, asserts they are absent from Keycloak's DB and present in the user-storage map, and logs in once with code index 0. It never reuses that code, never checks that the next login asks for the next index, never submits an out-of-order code, never regenerates codes after a local credential already exists, and never disables or deletes the credential. Those are the paths this PR gets wrong: isValid accepts any code and does not consume it, getCredentials rebuilds an unused set with a null id, disableCredentialType ignores the type, and a later user-storage create does not revoke an older local set. The test passes while recovery codes remain reusable and irremovable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before the new code that enables Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES. upgradeStrategy() yields null as well as RECREATE, and both testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount deploy that CR. The operator guide added in this change says that while the feature is preview, rolling-updates must be enabled or the Operator fails, and the CR example enables it even when strategy is left unset. The null cases therefore never put rolling-updates on spec.features.enabled. deployKeycloak(..., true) will time out if reconciliation fails closed without the feature. If the operator instead shells out to update-compatibility, that command now exits 4 (FEATURE_DISABLED) before it can report compatibility, so testCacheMaxCount(null) cannot observe the rolling update it asserts. Enable the feature for every strategy before that return. On the explicit-strategy path, setEnabledFeatures(List.of(rolling-updates)) also replaces any enabled-feature list already on the spec instead of adding rolling-updates, so other features configured by the test deployment would be dropped.

Exit code 4 is documented as a rolling-upgrade incompatibility

The check-command exit-code table says exit code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because rolling-updates is disabled. That is not what the implementation does. Both update-compatibility check and update-compatibility metadata return CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4) before any version or config comparison, after printing "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." The deployment may still be rolling-compatible; the tool refused to run. Exit code 3 uses the same "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" headline and tells the operator to shut the deployment down first. Scripts that follow this table and treat 4 like 3 will take unnecessary downtime, and a metadata-generation step that exits 4 will be misread as an upgrade incompatibility. Document 4 as a precondition failure for both subcommands: enable rolling-updates and re-run; do not shut down the cluster.

Remapped compatibility exit codes are not asserted

This change moves the recreate result from exit code 4 to 3 and assigns 4 to FEATURE_DISABLED, and the guide tells automation to rely on those codes rather than log text. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks that stderr contains the feature-disabled sentence; it never asserts exit code 4, and it only launches the metadata subcommand, not check, which has the same gate. testWrongVersions asserts the incompatibility text but not exit code 3, and the check invocation in testCompatible does not assert exit code 0. A regression that still prints the expected line but exits 4 for an incompatible version (the previous recreate code) or exits 1 after the feature-disabled message would pass CI and break scripts that branch on the exit code.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal still calls V2 setPermissionsEnabled, which throws

ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors all throw UnsupportedOperationException ("Not supported in V2"). This PR overrides MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() to return that class, and AdminPermissions.management prefers V2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. The removal listener still calls clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on ClientRemovedEvent when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is also enabled (the new guard only checks the V1 feature). Deleting a client then fails the transaction with UnsupportedOperationException instead of removing the client. If only V2 is enabled, the guard skips the listener and nothing deletes the per-client authorization resources this PR creates on the admin-permissions client (named by client id). Deleted clients leave orphaned resources and policies behind. setPermissionsEnabled should be a no-op under V2, and client removal should delete those V2 resources explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same V1-only feature flag guard on the removal listener and explains that enabling V2 without V1 skips cleanup, leaving orphaned authorization resources and policies. Its additional exception concern and client-specific remediation do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission does not return client ids

getClientsWithPermission is the allowlist API callers use to filter clients by scope. It adds resource.getName() for every type "Clients" resource whose evaluation grants the scope. The schema-level resource created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init is named "Clients", so an all-clients grant inserts the literal string "Clients" rather than every client id. Callers comparing the set to client.getId() or client.getClientId() will not treat that as access to all clients, and a clientId of "Clients" could be confused with the type resource. Object-level resources are named with the internal client id (resolveClient returns client.getId()), which already differs from V1, where this method returned clientId strings. In addition, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104) creates those resources with create/updateScopes and never setType, so findByType(CLIENTS) will not see them unless some other layer sets the type. Object-level grants are then omitted entirely. The method cannot be used to build a correct client allowlist.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: findByType only includes the type-level 'Clients' resource because per-client resources lack a type, and returning resource names therefore yields 'Clients' rather than actual client IDs. Although it describes different caller consequences, it matches the golden comment's incorrect client-ID allowlist concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing Clients type resource NPEs the permission check

When no per-client resource exists, hasPermission loads the type resource and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later resource.getScopes() with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the Clients resource was never created (init bails out when the admin-permissions client already exists) or if supportsAuthorizationSchema is false. findByResource dereferences resource.getId() and the permission check throws NullPointerException instead of returning false. An admin API call that should be denied becomes a 500. The same null resource is then passed to ResourcePermission if the isEmpty check were skipped.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing null check in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission: getResourceTypeResource can return null, which is passed to findByResource and causes a NullPointerException. Its additional details do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
All-clients permissions ignored once any per-client resource exists

ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String) evaluates the schema-level "Clients" resource only when resourceStore.findByName finds no resource named with that client's internal id. As soon as any object-level permission has created that resource, the method evaluates only the object resource and never loads all-clients policies. Those policies are stored on the separate "Clients" resource, and evaluatePermission is invoked with a ResourcePermission for only one resource, so they are not applied implicitly. Consequence: a manage/view/map-roles grant on all clients stops applying to a client as soon as anyone has any object-level permission on it (even a different scope or a different user). For example, an admin with manage-all loses manage, configure, and view on client X after another user is granted view on X. The same helper backs canManage, canConfigure, canView, canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles, and the new javadoc says those checks must also honor the all-clients scope. PermissionClientTest never combines an all-clients permission with an object-level permission on the same client, so this is untested.

Map-roles checks ignore manage-clients and cross-realm admins

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. Unlike canManage(ClientModel) in the same class, they never short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS). hasPermission then returns false immediately when root.isAdminSameRealm() is false, before any policy evaluation. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 makes AdminPermissions.evaluator/management always return MgmtPermissionsV2, so this class handles every admin request while the feature is on. Realm-management users who only have manage-clients, and master-realm admins managing another realm, are therefore denied mapping that client's roles, adding composite client roles, and mapping client-scope roles unless a fine-grained policy also exists. Those are ordinary admin operations. Callers that enforce these methods directly (requireMapRoles / requireMapCompositeRoles / requireMapClientScopeRoles) will return 403. The new tests only use myadmin, who has no manage-clients role, so the regression is not covered.

canExchangeTo throws instead of returning a decision

canExchangeTo unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. Token exchange decides whether the calling client may exchange for another client by invoking clients().canExchangeTo, and AdminPermissions.management returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, including for realms that have not turned on the new admin-permissions schema. The permission check therefore aborts the grant with an exception (typically a 500) instead of the boolean V1 returned. getEvaluationContext is implemented and unused, so the previous evaluation path was not wired up. A permission-check method must return false or delegate to super.canExchangeTo; it must not throw.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain Clients scopes

init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null. Scopes and type-level resources are created only on that path, from SCHEMA. This change adds the Clients resource type and the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes, but does not reconcile a client that was initialized when the schema contained only Users. On those realms the Clients resource and new scopes are never created. Creating a client permission then fails in getScope with ModelValidationException ("Scope [configure] does not exist") or in getOrCreateResource with ModelException ("No scopes found") when a required scope row is missing. Fresh enables work; any realm that already turned admin permissions on does not.

getResourceName does not resolve client resources

getResourceName special-cases Users: the type resource becomes "All users" and an object resource is resolved from the user id stored in resource.getName() to a username. There is no Clients branch. Client object resources are created with the internal client id as the name and no display name (getOrCreateResource only sets name, owner, and scopes). For a Clients policy the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null, instead of "All clients" or the clientId. Permission APIs that show which resource a policy applies to will return a null name for every client permission, and any caller that assumes a non-null display string can NPE. A missing client should be handled the same way a missing user is (ModelIllegalStateException), not silently omitted.

requireView javadoc describes a boolean return

The javadoc added on requireView says it "Returns true if canView() returns true", and requireViewClientScopes says it "Returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true". Both methods are void. They throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* check is false; they do not return a boolean. The comments document the wrong contract for every implementor of ClientPermissionEvaluator.

Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS JCA provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the provider of the default keystore type: SUN on Java 8 (JKS) and typically SunJSSE on later JDKs (PKCS12). Neither implements the ciphers, signatures, or BC algorithms callers request from this method. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null in the same situation. A non-null unrelated provider makes null-checks succeed, so Security.addProvider or Signature/Cipher.getInstance(alg, provider) runs against SUN/SunJSSE and throws NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently uses a non-BC implementation. This class is the provider selected for the standalone authz client, so any keycloak-core path that uses getBouncyCastleProvider() is wrong. Return null or throw; do not return the keystore provider.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore's provider rather than the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors

order() was added as a new abstract method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Any implementation not recompiled with this change (downstream forks, custom or test providers, an older provider jar still on the classpath) fails to compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader hits AbstractMethodError when detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order while sorting. That aborts crypto init and server startup. The same interface already uses default methods for optional behavior (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes). order() should default (for example to 0) so older implementors still load and lose to the in-repo providers that return 200.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding order() as an abstract method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied crypto providers are picked arbitrarily and no longer fail startup

detectProvider now sorts CryptoProviders by order() and, if more than one is found, only debug-logs the rest and returns foundProviders.get(0). The previous hard failure for multiple providers is gone. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so any two of them tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever ServiceLoader yielded first (classpath order), not a defined preference. ServiceLoader also constructs every provider before the sort, and FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at the front of the JVM security providers even when that implementation is then ignored. A classpath that contains more than one real provider — previously rejected at startup — can now run with the wrong CryptoProvider (including not actually being in FIPS mode) while FIPS JCA providers may already have been installed globally. Equal top order should still be a startup error.

AuthzClient.create can lock the JVM onto the stub crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; every later init is ignored for the life of the JVM. ServiceLoader is given the authz-client class loader, which always sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider (META-INF/services in this jar, order 100) but does not see providers that are only on a child or thread-context class loader. If create() runs before the server's own CryptoIntegration.init — embedded use, or a test that builds a client before server startup — the process is permanently stuck with AuthzClientCryptoProvider. That implementation throws UnsupportedOperationException for signature, PEM, certificate, cipher, and truststore operations. The new order() preference cannot correct this, because the higher-order provider was never visible to the class loader used for the first init. Creating a client should not freeze the process-wide provider on this stub.

ECDSA tests use a P-256 key and never check a real signature

The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JDK default curve (secp256r1). testES384 and testES512 still sign with that P-256 key while passing algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96 and 132) into the converter. ECDSA r/s width follows the curve order, not the JWS algorithm name, so those tests only round-trip 32-byte coordinates zero-padded to 48 or 66 bytes.
